284	                                 Results
285	                                 Search results
286	                                 The search strategy was conducted following PICOS guidelines49. Figure 1 shows the PRISMA 2020 flow diagram
287	                                 for study selection. A total of 5473 articles were retrieved from PubMed, the Cochrane Library, Web of Science,
288	                                 Scopus, Embase and Google Scholar databases. Two reviewers (JZ and SH) independently screened all titles and
289	                                 abstracts. Full texts of potentially eligible studies were then independently assessed by the same two reviewers.
290	                                 Disagreements at either stage were resolved through discussion or, if necessary, by consultation with a third
291	                                 reviewer (SL). Of the 30 full-text articles assessed, 16 were excluded for reasons presented in the PRISMA flow
292	                                 diagram (Fig. 1). The remaining 14 articles were included in the quantitative synthesis.
293	
294	                                 Quality and risk of bias assessment
295	                                 As a supplementary descriptive measure, PEDro scores for the 14 included studies ranged from 4 to 9 (Table 2),
296	                                 with corresponding descriptive categories based on established thresholds (9–10 = excellent, 6–8 = good,
297	                                 4–5 = fair, ≤ 3 = poor). One study scored 4 (fair), six studies scored 5–6 (five fair, one good), and seven studies
298	                                 scored 8–9 (good). These PEDro totals are presented for descriptive purposes only; all primary methodological
299	                                 quality assessments and GRADE downgrading decisions were based on the RoB 2 tool (Fig. 2; Supplementary
300	                                 Table 2).
301	                                      The RoB 2 assessment revealed substantial heterogeneity in methodological quality across the 14 included
302	                                 RCTs (Fig. 2). For each study, the overall risk-of-bias judgement was derived from the domain-level assessments
303	                                 of the primary outcome (TTRTP); for the small number of studies that also reported re-injury as a secondary
304	                                 outcome, the overall judgement did not differ materially, as the domains affecting TTRTP (randomization,
305	                                 deviations, and measurement) applied equally to the re-injury outcome. Figure 2 presents the overall study-
306	                                 level judgement; domain-level justifications are provided in Supplementary Table 2. Regarding specific domains,
307	                                 the randomization process was predominantly low risk, although approximately one-third showed some
308	                                 concerns due to unclear allocation concealment or baseline imbalances. Deviations from intended interventions
309	                                 constituted the major source of bias; in exercise-based trials, blinding of participants and personnel was
310	                                 unfeasible, which contributed to “some concerns” or “high risk” ratings when protocol deviations were judged
311	                                 likely to have arisen from the trial context (e.g. differential co-interventions or progression decisions influenced
312	                                 by knowledge of group allocation), consistent with RoB 2 guidance. Missing outcome data were generally low
313	                                 risk, with complete follow-up in most studies. Outcome measurement was largely low risk owing to assessor
314	                                 blinding, and selective reporting was judged as low risk for studies with available protocols, or some concerns
315	                                 where protocols were unavailable (see Supplementary Table 2 for domain-level justifications). These findings

                OPEN             Effects of rehabilitation
                                 interventions on time to return to
                                 play and reinjury rate in athletes
                                 with acute hamstring strain injuries
                                 Junshuai Zhu1,2, Shuaiwang Huang1, Shuyuan Luo1,2, Xinyun Huo1,2, Lan Zheng1,
                                 David Grecic2 & Xiyang Peng 1,2
                                 Despite the high prevalence and recurrence of acute hamstring strain injuries in athletes, the optimal
                                 rehabilitation strategy balancing rapid time to return to play (TTRTP) with durable re-injury protection
                                 remains unclear. We searched PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase, and Google
                                 Scholar from inception to January 2026 for English-language randomized controlled trials (RCTs)
                                 evaluating exercise-based rehabilitation, adjunctive biological modalities, or other approaches for
                                 acute hamstring strains in athletes. TTRTP was the primary outcome; re-injury rate was secondary.
                                 Certainty was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and
                                 Evaluation (GRADE). Models were selected based on heterogeneity and clinical plausibility of pooling.
                                 14 RCTs (693 athletes) were included. A lengthening-focused exercise protocol (L-protocol) based
                                 on two trials may shorten TTRTP versus conventional rehabilitation (moderate certainty) without
                                 increasing re-injury risk (low certainty). Progressive agility and trunk stabilization (PATS) did not
                                 accelerate TTRTP (low certainty); the re-injury estimate was inconclusive (RD -0.35, 95% CI -0.74 to
                                 0.03; I² = 72%; very low certainty; 2 trials), with the confidence interval including both a potential
                                 reduction and no effect. For adjunctive therapies, we analyzed Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) as a
                                 separate meta-analysis (three trials) and described radial extracorporeal shockwave therapy (rESWT)
                                 and low-level laser therapy (LLLT) as single-trial evidence. PRP showed heterogeneous effects (I²
                                 = 70%), rESWT modest benefit (one trial), and LLLT no added benefit (one trial). Pain-threshold
                                 rehab enhanced strength without delaying TTRTP (moderate certainty; one trial). Trial Sequential
                                 Analysis (TSA) indicated that the lengthening-focused exercise protocol (L-protocol) TTRTP benefit
                                 exceeded the monitoring boundary, suggesting sufficient evidence to rule out random error; however,
                                 this does not eliminate clinical heterogeneity or concerns about external validity. Lengthening-
                                 focused eccentric exercise may shorten TTRTP. Evidence for PATS and adjunctive modalities remains
                                 uncertain, warranting high-quality RCTs. Decisions should prioritize evidence certainty over statistical
                                 significance.

                                 Clinical trial registration: PROSPERO registration ID CRD420261387775.

                                 Keywords Hamstring strain injuries, Eccentric loading, Progressive agility and trunk stabilization, PRP,
                                 Time to return to play, Re-injury rate

                                 Hamstring strains (HSIs) are one of the most common injuries experienced by athletes in both contact and non-
                                 contact sports, with reported frequencies reaching up to 37% in some athletic populations1–4. Similar high injury
                                 rates have been observed in physically demanding occupational training, with up to 41% of recruits affected
                                 during initial phases5. Hamstring strains typically occur during movements involving extreme hip flexion and
                                 knee extension such as sprinting, jumping, or stretching3. The long head of the biceps femoris (BFlh) is most
                                 frequently affected, with injuries typically occurring 0–6 cm proximal to the myotendinous junction1. Acute
                                 HSIs present with localized pain and muscle fibre disruption (Grade I-III) of varying severity, which is associated
                                 with functional deficits2,6. This condition is distinct from proximal hamstring tendinopathy (an overuse disorder

Scientific Reports |   (2026) 16:30859               | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-70693-1                                                 1
 www.nature.com/scientificreports


                                 presenting with chronic deep gluteal pain during loaded activities), tendon avulsions (partial or complete
                                 detachment from the ischial tuberosity, often requiring surgical repair), recurrent strains (a repeat injury
                                 following an index strain), and delayed-onset posterior-thigh pain (non-traumatic muscle soreness without
                                 structural injury). These conditions differ in pathophysiology, natural history, and clinical management1. The
                                 high rates of HSIs have persisted for several decades, with some surveillance data indicating an approximate 4%
                                 annual increase in incidence in professional football populations7. HSIs occur more frequently during training
                                 than during competition and result in substantial time loss from sport, diminished athletic performance, and
                                 considerable economic burden8. Additionally, with a recurrence rate of 12–31%, HSIs present a significant
                                 challenge for athletes and clinicians alike9.
                                     Physical modalities and therapeutic exercises have been the subject of much research as traditional treatment
                                 options for HSIs over the last 20 years10,11. However, surgical intervention is usually only indicated for more
                                 serious or complicated cases12,13. The overall aim of rehabilitation from an HSI is the safe and timely return
                                 to athletic participation while reducing the chance of re-injury. This dual objective restoring function while
                                 mitigating recurrence risk is grounded in biomechanical principles that inform both performance optimization
                                 and injury prevention strategies. Therefore, clinicians treating athletes must be knowledgeable in evidence-based
                                 rehabilitation techniques to provide the athlete with the best possible therapeutic treatments, as well as improve
                                 their performance14–17.
                                     A range of adjunctive therapies, including orthobiologics such as platelet-rich plasma (PRP) and
                                 electrophysical agents such as low-level laser therapy (LLLT), radial extracorporeal shockwave therapy (rESWT),
                                 capacitive-resistive energy transfer (TECAR) and transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), is
                                 frequently employed alongside active rehabilitation12,18–20. However, these interventions differ substantially in
                                 their biological rationale, mechanisms of action and clinical objectives, and therefore should not be considered
                                 interchangeable21. PRP has been studied for its potential to deliver growth factors to injured tissue22,23. rESWT
                                 has been shown to help reduce TTRTP and increase recovery of strength24. Both TECAR and TENS have been
                                 shown to provide better short-term pain relief and improve flexibility than complete rest. However, studies
                                 examining the long-term efficacy of these modalities have produced limited data25. While physical modalities
                                 are used widely, their effectiveness as the sole treatment method is questionable at best; therefore, most studies
                                 examined physical modalities as part of a structured exercise program, and therefore the incremental benefit
                                 from exercise alone varies greatly by specific modality and stage of injury.
                                     Therapeutic exercise constitutes the cornerstone of HSI rehabilitation, grounded in a strong physiological
                                 rationale for restoring muscle strength, flexibility, neuromuscular control, and tissue capacity26,27. Contemporary
                                 exercise-based approaches have shifted from simple stretching and concentric strengthening toward more
                                 sophisticated protocols. Eccentric loading, particularly exercises performed at long muscle lengths has gained
                                 prominence due to its ability to increase fascicle length and enhance eccentric strength28. Another approach
                                 combines progressive agility exercises with trunk stabilization training (PATS), focusing on lumbopelvic
                                 control and movement patterns that mimic sporting actions18,29. Stretching exercises have traditionally been
                                 incorporated to restore range of motion; however, contemporary evidence suggests that static stretching alone
                                 provides limited functional benefit20,30,31. Current guidelines recommend stretching as an adjunct rather than
                                 a standalone intervention, with emphasis shifting toward eccentric loading and neuromuscular retraining32.
                                     The recent trend in clinical practice and research is towards combining physical modalities with exercise-
                                 based rehabilitation33,34, on the rationale that physical modalities may modulate pain and inflammation in the
                                 acute phase, thereby creating a more favorable environment for early loading35. In contrast, exercise therapy
                                 addresses the neuromuscular and biomechanical deficits that predispose athletes to recurrence-deficits that
                                 cannot be resolved by physical modalities alone. Preliminary evidence suggests that combined approaches
                                 may result in faster recovery than exercise alone, without increasing re-injury risk18,19,36. However, the optimal
                                 timing, sequencing, and combination of specific modalities with specific exercise protocols remain undefined,
                                 primarily due to variability in study design and outcome measures.
                                     Several recent systematic reviews have synthesized evidence on hamstring rehabilitation, but none have
                                 provided a stratified synthesis that separates exercise-based interventions from adjunctive therapies rather
                                 than pooling them, nor interpreted findings through both GRADE and TSA. This systematic review and meta-
                                 analysis therefore aimed to evaluate the efficacy of rehabilitation interventions for acute hamstring strain injuries
                                 in athletes, including eccentric loading, PATS and adjunctive biological and physical therapies. The primary
                                 outcome was time to return to play; secondary outcomes were re-injury rate, pain and functional recovery.
                                 Through this stratified synthesis, we sought to guide clinical decision making by evidence certainty rather than
                                 statistical significance alone.

                                 Methods
                                 This systematic review was conducted and reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement37.

                                 Inclusion criteria
                                 Studies were selected based on the following PICOS criteria. Population: competitive or recreational athletes with
                                 acute hamstring strain injuries, diagnosed clinically or by imaging; Intervention: (1) exercise-based rehabilitation
                                 programmes (eccentric loading, PATS, stretching); (2) adjunctive biological or physical therapies (PRP, rESWT,
                                 LLLT) when combined with structured rehabilitation; (3) stand-alone physical modalities (TECAR, TENS)
                                 evaluated as isolated treatments. Stand-alone modalities were included only for narrative synthesis and were not
                                 pooled in meta-analyses; Comparison: conventional rehabilitation, placebo, or alternative protocols; Outcomes:
                                 TTRTP (primary), re-injury rate, pain, and function (secondary); Study design: published RCTs (English-
                                 language only, due to resource constraints; acknowledged in Limitations).

                                 Exclusion criteria
                                 (1) Unpublished RCTs (including systematic reviews, meta-analyses, cross-sectional studies, observational
                                 studies, conference abstracts, case reports or non-randomized controlled trials). One master’s thesis was
                                 exceptionally included for narrative synthesis only because it provided unique data on an intervention not
                                 covered elsewhere (spinal adjustive therapy); its poor methodological quality (PEDro score 4) is acknowledged
                                 in the Limitations and it was not included in any pooled meta-analysis; (2) Studies where participants were not
                                 diagnosed with hamstring strain injury; (3) Studies that did not report any training or intervention measures; (4)
                                 Studies that did not report at least one of the prespecified outcomes (TTRTP, re-injury rate, pain, or functional
                                 outcomes); (5) Studies on chronic tendinopathy, tendon avulsions, or delayed-onset posterior-thigh pain.

                                 Literature search
                                 The search was conducted in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook and reported following the Preferred
                                 Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines37. Two reviewers (JZ
                                 and SH) independently performed the search and screened all retrieved records. The protocol for this review
                                 was registered with PROSPERO in May 2026 (CRD420261387775). The literature search was completed prior
                                 to registration, but screening against eligibility criteria and data extraction had not yet commenced. Screening
                                 began immediately after registration. The final analytical approach was consistent with the registered protocol,
                                 except for the post-hoc disaggregation of physical modalities (PRP, rESWT, LLLT), which is explicitly described
                                 in the Results. All other methods (eligibility criteria, outcomes, subgroup categories, analytical models, minimum
                                 clinically important difference, GRADE decisions, and TSA analyses) were established before screening began.
                                 From database inception to January 2026, PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase and
                                 Google Scholar databases were searched. The full search strategies for all databases, including controlled
                                 vocabulary, free-text terms, Boolean operators, field tags, and limits, are provided in Supplementary Table 1. In
                                 addition, three additional records were identified through screening the reference lists of included studies and
                                 relevant reviews. All studies were retrieved and imported into the citation database (EndNote 21), and duplicates
                                 were removed. The search terms are listed in Table 1.

                                 Quality and risk of bias assessment
                                 The risk of bias in the included RCTs was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool as the primary instrument38,
                                 with assessments conducted at the outcome level. Two reviewers independently evaluated each study across five
                                 domains: randomization process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement
                                 of the outcome, and selection of the reported result. Each domain was rated as “low risk of bias”, “some
                                 concerns” or “high risk of bias” following standard RoB 2 guidance. Domain-level justifications are provided in
                                 Supplementary Table 2. Judgements for selective reporting were based on available trial registrations or published
                                 protocols where accessible; otherwise, the domain was rated as “some concerns” in the absence of a pre-registered
                                 protocol. For exercise-based trials, lack of blinding of participants and personnel was not automatically rated as
                                 high risk; rather, ratings reflected whether protocol deviations (e.g. differential co-interventions or progression
                                 decisions influenced by knowledge of allocation) were judged likely given the trial context, consistent with RoB
                                 2 guidance38. In addition, we used the PEDro scale to describe the methodological quality of included studies as
                                 a supplementary descriptive measure, not as a primary risk-of-bias tool.

                                 Data analysis
                                 Data from the fourteen studies were independently extracted by two reviewers and recorded in Microsoft
                                 Excel 2025 spreadsheets to facilitate the comparison and interpretation of research findings. The extracted data
                                 encompassed participant characteristics (age, sex, and type of exercise), sample sizes for each assigned group,
                                 administered intervention protocols, and the follow-up duration. A consensus on all extracted data was reached
                                 by both authors prior to subsequent analysis. We preferentially extracted intention-to-treat data when available.
                                 For the single study reporting medians and IQRs (Hamilton et al.39), the SD was estimated using IQR/1.35. No
                                 authors were contacted for missing data, and no imputation was required. Inter-reviewer agreement was high
                                 (Cohen’s κ = 0.92). Data analysis was performed using Review Manager (RevMan) version 5.4. Model selection
                                 followed a prespecified strategy: random-effects models were used as the primary approach for all meta-
                                 analyses where clinical transitivity was judged adequate, to account for anticipated clinical and methodological
                                 heterogeneity across the included trials, including variations in study populations, intervention protocols, and
                                 outcome definitions. Fixed-effects models were used only in sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness of
                                 findings under an alternative modelling assumption. For TTRTP analyses, we used random-effects models with

                                 inverse variance weighting. For re-injury analyses, we used Mantel-Haenszel risk difference with random-effect
                                 models as the primary approach, consistent with recommendations for sparse binary data40. The random-effects
                                 estimator was DerSimonian-Laird, with confidence intervals based on the standard normal approximation.
                                 Heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic; I² > 50% was considered a guide for substantial heterogeneity,
                                 but clinical and methodological heterogeneity particularly variations in return-to-play definitions and re-
                                 injury surveillance periods was assessed qualitatively before examining statistical heterogeneity. In the analysis
                                 evaluating the impact of hamstring eccentric loading and the hamstring strengthening program combined with
                                 progressive agility and trunk stabilization on TTRTP, the weighted mean difference (WMD) was employed to
                                 calculate the pooled effect size, owing to the utilization of identical measurement criteria. Risk difference (RD)
                                 was utilized to evaluate the re-injury rates between the intervention and control groups. Risk ratio (RR) was
                                 applied in subgroup analyses to examine the influence of follow-up duration on re-injury rates41. Heterogeneity
                                 among studies was assessed using the Q statistic and the I² index, with the significance level established at
                                 p < 0.05. The I² index quantifies heterogeneity, with values of ≤ 25%, > 25% to ≤ 50%, and > 50% indicative of low,
                                 moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively.
                                     In sensitivity analyses, we additionally applied Peto odds ratio, which is more stable with sparse events42,43.
                                 Studies with zero events in both arms were not estimable and did not contribute to pooled estimates. For
                                 outcomes with few studies and events, results were interpreted with emphasis on confidence intervals rather
                                 than p-values. Sensitivity analyses examined the influence of effect measure (RD versus OR) and model choice
                                 on conclusions. For multi-arm trials, only relevant arms were included: for the three-arm Hamilton trial, we
                                 used only the PRP and no-injection groups to avoid double-counting. No missing data required imputation,
                                 as all continuous outcomes were reported as means with standard deviations. Outcomes were extracted at the
                                 primary TTRTP endpoint prespecified in each trial. The analytical approach followed the PROSPERO-registered
                                 protocol, except for the post-hoc disaggregation of physical modalities (PRP, rESWT, LLLT), which is explicitly
                                 described in the Results. For the three-arm Hamilton trial (PRP, PPP, and no injection), we included only the
                                 PRP and no-injection groups in the meta-analysis. The PPP arm was excluded to avoid double-counting, and the
                                 no-injection group was selected as the comparator because it represented rehabilitation alone, consistent with
                                 the other PRP trials. No participants were double-counted.

                                 Synthesis without meta-analysis
                                 For outcomes and intervention categories that could not be pooled in meta-analysis (pain-threshold
                                 rehabilitation, stand-alone physical modalities, stretching exercises, and spinal adjustive therapy), we conducted
                                 a narrative synthesis following the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) reporting guideline44. Findings are
                                 presented descriptively with effect estimates and confidence intervals transcribed verbatim from the original
                                 reports. No additional statistical pooling was performed for these comparisons.

                                 Sensitivity analyses
                                 To assess robustness, we compared fixed-effects versus random-effects models, RD versus Peto OR as alternative
                                 effect measures, and examined the influence of continuity correction (adding 0.5 to all cells) for zero-event
                                 studies. Results were considered robust if direction and significance remained consistent across sensitivity
                                 analyses. Fixed-effects models were applied as a sensitivity analysis to examine whether the primary findings
                                 were robust to alternative modelling assumptions. Results were considered robust if the direction and magnitude
                                 of effect remained consistent across random- and fixed-effects models.

                                 Trial sequential analysis
                                 Trial sequential analysis (TSA) was performed to quantify the risk of random error in cumulative meta-analyses45,
                                 thereby serving as a robustness check for the primary meta-analytic conclusions. The required information size
                                 (RIS) was calculated using α = 0.05, β = 0.20, with control event proportions and effect estimates derived from
                                 the included trials; diversity-adjusted RIS was used for TTRTP outcomes to account for heterogeneity, while
                                 the re-injury analyses used the control event proportion from the pooled data due to sparse events. RIS values
                                 are provided in the figure legends for each TSA plot. The O’Brien-Fleming monitoring boundary was applied
                                 for all TSA plots; futility boundaries were not used. Conventional meta-analysis declares statistical significance
                                 when the Z-curve crosses ± 1.96 (the conventional boundary for P < 0.05). TSA imposes more stringent O’Brien-
                                 Fleming boundaries: crossing the monitoring boundary before reaching RIS indicates sufficient evidence;
                                 crossing the conventional 1.96 boundary but not the TSA boundary suggests potential false-positive results due
                                 to sparse data46. TSA was conducted using TSA 0.9.5.10 Beta, with trials entered in chronological order for each
                                 meta-analysis.

                                 Grading of evidence quality using the GRADE approach
                                 To evaluate the overall certainty of evidence for TTRTP and Re-injury outcomes, we applied the GRADE
                                 framework. Two reviewers independently rated the evidence using GRADEpro, with disagreements resolved by a
                                 third reviewer47,48. Evidence quality was downgraded for serious limitations in risk of bias (RoB 2), inconsistency
                                 (I² > 50%), indirectness, or imprecision. Publication bias was not formally assessed due to the limited number
                                 of studies per comparison (≤ 5). Upgrading was not applied as all evidence originated from RCTs, which begin
                                 at high certainty. For TTRTP, we prespecified a 7-day MCID. This threshold was established a priori in our
                                 PROSPERO protocol, is consistent with sample-size calculations used in prior hamstring rehabilitation trials39,
                                 and reflects the clinical judgment that a one-week reduction in RTP time is meaningful in athletic populations.
                                 Imprecision was judged by whether the 95% confidence interval crossed this MCID threshold, in addition to
                                 examining confidence interval width.

                                 Results
                                 Search results
                                 The search strategy was conducted following PICOS guidelines49. Figure 1 shows the PRISMA 2020 flow diagram
                                 for study selection. A total of 5473 articles were retrieved from PubMed, the Cochrane Library, Web of Science,
                                 Scopus, Embase and Google Scholar databases. Two reviewers (JZ and SH) independently screened all titles and
                                 abstracts. Full texts of potentially eligible studies were then independently assessed by the same two reviewers.
                                 Disagreements at either stage were resolved through discussion or, if necessary, by consultation with a third
                                 reviewer (SL). Of the 30 full-text articles assessed, 16 were excluded for reasons presented in the PRISMA flow
                                 diagram (Fig. 1). The remaining 14 articles were included in the quantitative synthesis.

                                 Quality and risk of bias assessment
                                 As a supplementary descriptive measure, PEDro scores for the 14 included studies ranged from 4 to 9 (Table 2),
                                 with corresponding descriptive categories based on established thresholds (9–10 = excellent, 6–8 = good,
                                 4–5 = fair, ≤ 3 = poor). One study scored 4 (fair), six studies scored 5–6 (five fair, one good), and seven studies
                                 scored 8–9 (good). These PEDro totals are presented for descriptive purposes only; all primary methodological
                                 quality assessments and GRADE downgrading decisions were based on the RoB 2 tool (Fig. 2; Supplementary
                                 Table 2).
                                      The RoB 2 assessment revealed substantial heterogeneity in methodological quality across the 14 included
                                 RCTs (Fig. 2). For each study, the overall risk-of-bias judgement was derived from the domain-level assessments
                                 of the primary outcome (TTRTP); for the small number of studies that also reported re-injury as a secondary
                                 outcome, the overall judgement did not differ materially, as the domains affecting TTRTP (randomization,
                                 deviations, and measurement) applied equally to the re-injury outcome. Figure 2 presents the overall study-
                                 level judgement; domain-level justifications are provided in Supplementary Table 2. Regarding specific domains,
                                 the randomization process was predominantly low risk, although approximately one-third showed some
                                 concerns due to unclear allocation concealment or baseline imbalances. Deviations from intended interventions
                                 constituted the major source of bias; in exercise-based trials, blinding of participants and personnel was
                                 unfeasible, which contributed to “some concerns” or “high risk” ratings when protocol deviations were judged
                                 likely to have arisen from the trial context (e.g. differential co-interventions or progression decisions influenced
                                 by knowledge of group allocation), consistent with RoB 2 guidance. Missing outcome data were generally low
                                 risk, with complete follow-up in most studies. Outcome measurement was largely low risk owing to assessor
                                 blinding, and selective reporting was judged as low risk for studies with available protocols, or some concerns
                                 where protocols were unavailable (see Supplementary Table 2 for domain-level justifications). These findings

417	                                          Transfer energy capacitive and resistive, TENS Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, VAS visual
418	                                          analogue scale, FASH functional assessment for acute hamstring injuries, SLR straight leg raise, STR sit-and-
419	                                          reach test, TTRTP time to return to play, L-protocol lengthening protocol, C-protocol conventional protocol,
420	                                          PATS Progressive agility and trunk stabilization, PRES Progressive running and eccentric strengthening, STST
421	                                          stretching and strengthening, ROM range of motion, rESWT radial extracorporeal shock wave therapy, RP
422	                                          rehabilitation program, PRP platelet-rich plasma, PPP platelet‑poor plasma, WB whole blood, r/a randomized/

427	                                          indicate that methodological quality varied considerably, underscoring the need for cautious interpretation of
428	                                          meta-analytic results, particularly from studies with high risk of bias, and highlight the importance of improved
429	                                          reporting standards in future trials.
430	
431	                                          Study characteristics
432	                                          According to Table 2, a total of 693 participants diagnosed with hamstring injuries were included in this study,
433	                                          with mean participant ages across studies ranging from 20.3 years to 46.6 years. Most of the participants were
434	                                          professional, and semi-professional athletes engaged in sports such as football and track and field, and most
435	                                          diagnoses (10/14 studies) were confirmed by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or ultrasound imaging.
436	                                          Most included studies reported TTRTP and re-injury rate as primary or secondary outcomes; two studies25,54
437	                                          reported only short-term functional outcomes without formal TTRTP data and were therefore excluded from
438	
439	
440	Scientific Reports |       (2026) 16:30859                             | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-70693-1                                                                     6
441	 www.nature.com/scientificreports
442	
443	
444	
445	
446	                                 Fig. 2. Risk of bias assessment (RoB 2 domains: (1) Randomization process; (2) Deviation from intended
447	                                 interventions; (3) Missing outcome data; (4) Measurement of the outcome; (5) Selection of the reported result;
448	                                 (6) Overall risk of bias). Domain-level justifications are provided in Supplementary Table 2.
449	
450	
451	
452	                                 the quantitative synthesis. TTRTP definitions varied across studies and are detailed in Table 2. Re-injury was
453	                                 generally defined as a repeat hamstring injury after return to sport, with follow-up periods of 2–24 months. Except
454	                                 for Hickey et al.58, who included the degree of pain as an element in their study, all the other trials’ intervention
455	                                 items were carried out without pain. A part of the included studies mainly focused on evaluating the effects of
456	                                 therapeutic rehabilitation training, including strength enhancement and stretching load exercises. Two studies
457	                                 evaluated the hamstring loading training performed during stretching exercises50,51. Two studies evaluated the
458	                                 hamstring strengthening training program combined with progressive agility and trunk stability training52,53.
459	                                 Five studies evaluated the effect of combining rehabilitation programs with physical therapy39,56,57,59,61. Among
460	                                 them, three studies were about PRP39,57,61, one was about rESWT59, and one was about LLLT56. Kelli et al.25
461	                                 evaluated the therapeutic effects of TECAR, TENS on HSIs from a single modality perspective. Regarding
462	                                 stretching, Sefiddashti et al.55 and Malliaropoulos et al.60 respectively evaluated the therapeutic effects of
463	                                 combining cold therapy with stretching and increasing the frequency of stretching. One more research report
464	                                 presented the therapeutic effect of spinal adjustive therapy54.
465	
466	                                 Meta-analysis results
467	                                 The data synthesis was structured according to the primary intervention categories identified in the included
468	                                 studies: (I) hamstring eccentric loading; (II) hamstring strengthening combined with progressive agility and
469	                                 trunk stabilization; (III) rehabilitation program combined with PRP. For each category, the effects on TTRTP,
470	                                 re‑injury rate, and pain/functional outcomes were analyzed separately. Heterogeneity was assessed using the I²
471	                                 statistic, and effect sizes were calculated as weighted mean difference (WMD), standardized mean difference
472	                                 (SMD), risk difference (RD) or risk ratio (RR) as appropriate.
473	
474	
475	
476	
477	Scientific Reports |   (2026) 16:30859               | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-70693-1                                                   7
478	 www.nature.com/scientificreports
479	
480	
481	
482	
483	                                 Fig. 3. Forest plot of the impact of L-protocol and C-protocol on TTRTP of HSIs; TTRTP time to return to
484	                                 play; WMD weighted mean difference; CI confidence interval.
485	
486	
487	
488	
489	                                 Fig. 4. Forest plot of the impact of L-protocol and C-protocol on re-injury rate of HSIs; RD risk difference; CI
490	                                 confidence interval.
491	
492	
493	
494	                                 Hamstring eccentric loading
495	                                 TTRTP
496	                                 Two randomized controlled trials50,51 evaluated the effect of a lengthening-protocol (L-protocol) compared with
497	                                 a conventional protocol (C-protocol) on TTRTP following acute hamstring strains. A random-effects meta-
498	                                 analysis was conducted due to moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 58%, P = 0.12). The pooled results showed that
499	                                 the L-protocol significantly reduced TTRTP compared with the C-protocol, with a weighted mean difference
500	                                 (WMD) of −28.29 days (95% CI −41.60 to −14.99, p < 0.0001; Fig. 3). Askling et al.50 reported a mean difference
501	                                 of −23.00 days (95% CI −31.24 to −14.76) in elite football players, while Askling et al.51 observed a larger effect
502	                                 (−37.00 days, 95% CI −52.85 to −21.15) in Swedish elite sprinters and jumpers. These findings indicate that a
503	                                 rehabilitation protocol emphasizing lengthening exercises (L-protocol) may accelerate TTRTP compared with
504	                                 conventional rehabilitation.
505	
506	                                 Re-injury rate
507	                                 These two studies50,51 reported re-injury rate following L-protocol versus C-protocol in athletes with HSIs. A
508	                                 fixed-effects meta-analysis using MH-RD was performed (I2 = 0%, P = 0.48). No significant difference was found
509	                                 between groups (RD −0.05, 95% CI −0.11 to 0.02, p = 0.17; Fig. 4). No re-injuries occurred in the L-protocol
510	                                 group (0/65), whereas the C-protocol group had three (3/66). A sensitivity analysis using Peto OR confirmed
511	                                 the null finding (OR 0.13, 95% CI 0.01 to 1.30, p = 0.08), supporting robustness. These findings indicate a trend
512	                                 toward reduced re-injury risk with the L-protocol compared with conventional rehabilitation.
513	
514	                                 Pain and functional outcomes
515	                                 Neither of the two included studies on hamstring eccentric loading systematically reported quantitative pain
516	                                 scores (e.g. visual analogue scale) or standardized functional outcome measures (e.g. functional assessment
517	                                 for HSIs) as primary or secondary endpoints. Both studies used pain‑guided rehabilitation progression, where
518	                                 exercises were performed without pain provocation. Clinical recovery was monitored weekly through manual
519	                                 assessment of flexibility (passive straight leg raise) and isometric strength, with the absence of localised palpation
520	                                 pain and pain during isometric contraction serving as criteria for advancing to the next rehabilitation stage50.
521	                                 Additionally, the Askling H‑test-a dynamic test assessing the player’s confidence and absence of insecurity
522	                                 during a simulated high‑speed running movement-was applied prior to return to sport. In the L‑protocol
523	                                 group, 35% of players (13/37) experienced insecurity and required an average extension of 7.5 days (SD ± 2.8) of
524	                                 rehabilitation, compared with 71% (27/38) in the C‑protocol group (mean extension 6.7 days, SD ± 2.7)50. These
525	                                 findings suggest that the L‑protocol was associated with fewer functional deficits at the time of return‑to‑play
526	                                 testing; however, due to the absence of uniform pain or functional scales, a quantitative meta‑analysis was not
527	                                 feasible for this outcome domain.
528	
529	                                 Hamstring strengthening program combined with progressive agility and trunk stabilization
530	                                 For PATS analyses, the two included trials used different control interventions STST (stretching and strengthening)
531	                                 and PRES (progressive running and eccentric strengthening) both of which represent conventional rehabilitation
532	                                 approaches. We considered pooling these comparisons clinically appropriate as both reflect standard care against
533	                                 which PATS was evaluated.
534	
535	
536	
537	
538	Scientific Reports |   (2026) 16:30859               | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-70693-1                                                    8
539	 www.nature.com/scientificreports
540	
541	
542	
543	
544	                                 Fig. 5. Forest plot of the impact of PATS and control programs (STST or PRES) on TTRTP of HSIs; TTRTP
545	                                 time to return to play; WMD weighted mean difference; CI confidence interval.
546	
547	
548	
549	
550	                                 Fig. 6. Forest plot of the impact of PATS and control programs (STST or PRES) on re-injury rate of HSIs; RD
551	                                 risk difference; CI confidence interval.
552	
553	
554	
555	                                 TTRTP
556	                                 Two randomized controlled trials52,53 evaluated the effect of a PATS compared with STST or PRES on TTRTP
557	                                 following HSIs. A random-effects meta-analysis was performed due to moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 35%,
558	                                 P = 0.21). The pooled analysis showed no significant difference in TTRTP between the PATS group and the
559	                                 control groups, with a WMD of −6.72 days (95% CI −16.81 to 3.36, p = 0.19; Fig. 5). Sherry et al.53 reported a
560	                                 mean difference of − 15.20 days (95% CI −32.12 to 1.72) favoring PATS over STST, whereas Silder et al.52 found
561	                                 a smaller, non-significant difference of −3.60 days (95% CI −10.52 to 3.32) when comparing PATS with PRES.
562	                                 These findings indicate that, compared with conventional strengthening and stretching or eccentric running
563	                                 programs, the addition of progressive agility and trunk stabilization does not significantly accelerate return to
564	                                 sport after HSIs.
565	
566	                                 Re-injury rate
567	                                 These two studies52,53 reported re-injury rate following PATS compared with STST or PRES. A random-effects
568	                                 meta-analysis using risk difference was conducted due to substantial heterogeneity (Tau² = 0.06; Chi² = 3.54,
569	                                 df = 1, P = 0.06; I² = 72%). The pooled analysis showed no statistically significant difference in re-injury rate
570	                                 between PATS and control groups (RD −0.35, 95% CI −0.74 to 0.03, p = 0.07; Fig. 6). Across both studies, two
571	                                 re-injuries occurred in the PATS groups (n = 29) compared with ten in the control groups (n = 24). Individual
572	                                 trial results ranged from RD −0.56 (95% CI −0.88 to −0.24) in Sherry et al.53 to RD −0.17 (95% CI −0.43 to 0.09)
573	                                 in Silder et al.52. A sensitivity analysis using Peto odds ratio (I² = 0%) yielded a larger effect estimate (OR 0.08,
574	                                 95% CI 0.02 to 0.38), but the statistical significance of this estimate should be interpreted with caution. The Peto
575	                                 odds ratio can produce unstable estimates in the presence of very large treatment effects and sparse event data,
576	                                 as is the case here. The primary analysis using risk difference (RD −0.35, 95% CI −0.74 to 0.03, p = 0.07) was
577	                                 statistically inconclusive, and the inconsistent findings across the two analytical approaches indicate that the
578	                                 evidence for PATS on re-injury prevention remains uncertain. We therefore emphasize the absolute event counts
579	                                 (2/29 vs. 10/24) and the width of the RD confidence interval, which crosses the null, as more informative than
580	                                 the point estimate of the Peto OR.
581	
582	                                 Pain and Functional Outcomes
583	                                 Sherry et al.53 conducted a battery of functional tests at the TTRTP, including hop tests (hop for height, hop
584	                                 for distance, 4-hop crossover test) and 40-yard sprint times. No significant differences were observed between
585	                                 the PATS and STST groups for any functional measure (all p > 0.05). Furthermore, functional test performance
586	                                 did not differ between athletes who subsequently sustained a re-injury and those who did not (P = 0.07–0.97),
587	                                 suggesting that these tests had limited predictive value for re-injury risk. Silder et al.52 reported that at the
588	                                 TTRTP, nearly all subjects in both groups had resolution of pain with palpation and during manual muscle
589	                                 strength testing. However, 11 of 25 subjects (44%) who completed rehabilitation reported remaining hamstring
590	                                 symptoms (e.g. pain, tightness), with no significant difference between groups (7/13 in PATS vs. 4/12 in PRES,
591	                                 P = 0.444). Twelve subjects (48%) did not feel they had returned to their pre-injury level of performance, though
592	                                 only three (12%) attributed this limitation to their hamstring injury, with general deconditioning being the
593	                                 most common limiting factor. ROM measures (passive straight leg raise) showed no significant between-group
594	                                 differences at final examination (P = 0.337). Importantly, despite meeting clinical return-to-sport criteria (no
595	                                 pain, full strength), no subject in either group showed complete resolution of injury on MRI, indicating ongoing
596	                                 tissue healing52,53.
597	
598	
599	
600	Scientific Reports |   (2026) 16:30859               | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-70693-1                                                   9
601	 www.nature.com/scientificreports
602	
603	
604	
605	
606	                                 Fig. 7. Forest plot of the impact of PRP combined with rehabilitation versus rehabilitation alone (no injection)
607	                                 on TTRTP of HSIs; TTRTP time to return to play; WMD weighted mean difference; CI confidence interval.
608	
609	
610	
611	
612	                                 Fig. 8. Forest plot of the impact of PRP combined with rehabilitation versus rehabilitation alone (no injection)
613	                                 on re-injury rate of HSIs; RD risk difference; CI confidence interval.
614	
615	
616	
617	                                    Taken together, these findings indicate that PATS and control programs yield comparable improvements in
618	                                 pain and functional performance at the TTRTP. However, residual symptoms and functional deficits may persist
619	                                 despite clinical clearance, underscoring the need for continued monitoring and gradual return to full activity.
620	
621	                                 Rehabilitation programs combined with physical modalities
622	                                 Five randomized controlled trials39,56,57,59,61 evaluated the effect of rehabilitation programs combined with
623	                                 physical modalities on TTRTP following HSIs. Due to substantial differences in biological rationale, mechanism
624	                                 of action, and clinical objectives, we did not pool these interventions into a single estimate. Instead, we conducted
625	                                 a meta-analysis for PRP, for which three trials were available, and narratively described the single-trial evidence
626	                                 for rESWT and LLLT.
627	
628	                                 Rehabilitation programs combined with PRP
629	                                 TTRTP
630	                                 A random-effects meta-analysis of the three PRP trials (PRP combined with rehabilitation versus rehabilitation
631	                                 alone or placebo injection) showed that PRP suggestively reduced TTRTP compared with control, with a
632	                                 weighted mean difference (WMD) of −6.77 days (95% CI −10.79 to −2.75, p = 0.0010; Fig. 7). Heterogeneity was
633	                                 substantial (I² = 70%, p = 0.03). Individual trial effects ranged from WMD − 4.00 days (95% CI −6.48 to −1.52)
634	                                 in Hamilton et al.39 to WMD − 15.80 days (95% CI −28.11 to −3.49) in Hamid et al.61, with Desouza et al.57
635	                                 reporting an intermediate effect (WMD − 7.80 days, 95% CI −10.40 to −5.20). The substantial heterogeneity may
636	                                 reflect differences in PRP preparation (leukocyte-rich versus leukocyte-poor), injection timing, rehabilitation
637	                                 protocols, or definitions of return to sport across studies.
638	
639	                                 Re-injury rate
640	                                 The three PRP trials reported re-injury rates over follow-up periods ranging from 6 to 24 months. A fixed-effects
641	                                 meta-analysis (I² = 0%, p = 0.32) showed no significant difference between PRP and control groups (RD −0.08,
642	                                 95% CI −0.19 to 0.02, p = 0.13; Fig. 8). Across the three trials, three re-injuries occurred in the PRP groups
643	                                 (n = 56) versus eight in controls (n = 59). Sensitivity analyses using Peto OR (OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.12 to 1.34,
644	                                 p = 0.14) and random-effects models (OR 0.39, 95% CI 0.11 to 1.36) confirmed the null finding. Desouza et al.57
645	                                 reported one re-injury in the PRP group versus five in controls (RD −0.13, 95% CI −0.28 to 0.01); Hamilton et
646	                                 al.39 reported two versus three (RD −0.03, 95% CI −0.18 to 0.12); Hamid et al.61 reported no re-injuries in either
647	                                 group and did not contribute to the pooled estimate.
648	
649	                                 Pain and functional outcomes
650	                                 Hamid et al.61 assessed pain using the Brief Pain Inventory-Short Form (BPI-SF). Patients in the PRP group
651	                                 demonstrated significantly lower pain severity scores across all follow up time points compared with controls (β
652	                                 = −0.390, 95% CI −0.67 to −0.11, p = 0.007). However, no significant between-group difference was observed for
653	                                 pain interference with daily activities (β = −0.185, 95% CI −0.44 to 0.07, p = 0.157). Hamilton et al.39 evaluated
654	                                 isokinetic knee flexor strength at return to sport and found no significant differences between PRP and control
655	                                 groups for concentric strength at 60°/s, 300°/s, or eccentric strength at 60°/s (all p > 0.05). Desouza et al.57 did not
656	                                 report standardized pain or functional outcome measures. Due to the heterogeneity in outcome reporting across
657	                                 studies, a quantitative synthesis for pain and functional outcomes was not feasible.
658	
659	
660	Scientific Reports |   (2026) 16:30859                | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-70693-1                                                   10
661	 www.nature.com/scientificreports
662	
663	
664	                                 Rehabilitation programs combined with rESWT
665	                                 TTRTP
666	                                 The rESWT group showed a significantly shorter TTRTP compared with the sham group (25.4 ± 3.5 days versus
667	                                 28.3 ± 4.5 days; mean difference − 2.90 days, 95% CI −5.63 to −0.17; SMD − 0.70, 95% CI −1.38 to −0.03).
668	
669	                                 Re-injury rate
670	                                 One re-injury occurred in each group over the 6-month follow-up period (1/16 versus 1/16), with no significant
671	                                 between-group difference. Due to single-trial nature, formal meta-analysis was not performed.
672	
673	                                 Pain and functional outcomes
674	                                 Crupnik et al.59 assessed isometric knee flexor strength post-treatment using two-way repeated measures
675	                                 ANOVA. A significant leg effect (previously injured versus contralateral uninjured leg) was observed (p = 0.005),
676	                                 but no significant treatment effect was detected (p = 0.899). Post-hoc testing showed that in the sham rESWT
677	                                 group, the previously injured leg was significantly weaker than the contralateral uninjured leg (p = 0.014),
678	                                 whereas no such difference was observed in the rESWT group. However, the treatment-by-leg interaction was
679	                                 not reported; therefore, these findings should be interpreted cautiously and do not establish that rESWT restores
680	                                 strength symmetry.
681	
682	                                 Rehabilitation programs combined with LLLT
683	                                 TTRTP
684	                                 The study found no significant benefit of LLLT over placebo for TTRTP (mean difference − 0.80 days, 95% CI
685	                                 −11.22 to 9.62; SMD − 0.06, 95% CI −0.90 to 0.77).
686	
687	                                 Re-injury rate
688	                                 No re-injuries occurred in either group during the 6-month follow-up period (0/11 versus 0/11). With zero
689	                                 events in both arms, the effect estimate was not estimable.
690	
691	                                 Pain and functional outcomes
692	                                 Medeiros et al.56 assessed hamstring flexibility (passive straight leg raise, knee extension test, maximal hip flexion
693	                                 active knee extension) and isometric strength (inner, mid, and outer range) using a handheld dynamometer.
694	                                 Both the LLLT and placebo groups showed significant improvements over time (time effect p < 0.05), but no

                                 The data synthesis was structured according to the primary intervention categories identified in the included

                                 trunk stabilization; (III) rehabilitation program combined with PRP. For each category, the effects on TTRTP,
                                 re‑injury rate, and pain/functional outcomes were analyzed separately. Heterogeneity was assessed using the I²
                                 statistic, and effect sizes were calculated as weighted mean difference (WMD), standardized mean difference
                                 (SMD), risk difference (RD) or risk ratio (RR) as appropriate.

                                 Hamstring eccentric loading
                                 TTRTP
                                 Two randomized controlled trials50,51 evaluated the effect of a lengthening-protocol (L-protocol) compared with
                                 a conventional protocol (C-protocol) on TTRTP following acute hamstring strains. A random-effects meta-
                                 analysis was conducted due to moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 58%, P = 0.12). The pooled results showed that
                                 the L-protocol significantly reduced TTRTP compared with the C-protocol, with a weighted mean difference
                                 (WMD) of −28.29 days (95% CI −41.60 to −14.99, p < 0.0001; Fig. 3). Askling et al.50 reported a mean difference
                                 of −23.00 days (95% CI −31.24 to −14.76) in elite football players, while Askling et al.51 observed a larger effect
                                 (−37.00 days, 95% CI −52.85 to −21.15) in Swedish elite sprinters and jumpers. These findings indicate that a
                                 rehabilitation protocol emphasizing lengthening exercises (L-protocol) may accelerate TTRTP compared with
                                 conventional rehabilitation.

                                 Re-injury rate
                                 These two studies50,51 reported re-injury rate following L-protocol versus C-protocol in athletes with HSIs. A
                                 fixed-effects meta-analysis using MH-RD was performed (I2 = 0%, P = 0.48). No significant difference was found
                                 between groups (RD −0.05, 95% CI −0.11 to 0.02, p = 0.17; Fig. 4). No re-injuries occurred in the L-protocol
                                 group (0/65), whereas the C-protocol group had three (3/66). A sensitivity analysis using Peto OR confirmed
                                 the null finding (OR 0.13, 95% CI 0.01 to 1.30, p = 0.08), supporting robustness. These findings indicate a trend
                                 toward reduced re-injury risk with the L-protocol compared with conventional rehabilitation.

                                 Pain and functional outcomes
                                 Neither of the two included studies on hamstring eccentric loading systematically reported quantitative pain
                                 scores (e.g. visual analogue scale) or standardized functional outcome measures (e.g. functional assessment
                                 for HSIs) as primary or secondary endpoints. Both studies used pain‑guided rehabilitation progression, where
                                 exercises were performed without pain provocation. Clinical recovery was monitored weekly through manual
                                 assessment of flexibility (passive straight leg raise) and isometric strength, with the absence of localised palpation
                                 pain and pain during isometric contraction serving as criteria for advancing to the next rehabilitation stage50.
                                 Additionally, the Askling H‑test-a dynamic test assessing the player’s confidence and absence of insecurity
                                 during a simulated high‑speed running movement-was applied prior to return to sport. In the L‑protocol
                                 group, 35% of players (13/37) experienced insecurity and required an average extension of 7.5 days (SD ± 2.8) of
                                 rehabilitation, compared with 71% (27/38) in the C‑protocol group (mean extension 6.7 days, SD ± 2.7)50. These
                                 findings suggest that the L‑protocol was associated with fewer functional deficits at the time of return‑to‑play
                                 testing; however, due to the absence of uniform pain or functional scales, a quantitative meta‑analysis was not
                                 feasible for this outcome domain.

                                 Hamstring strengthening program combined with progressive agility and trunk stabilization
                                 For PATS analyses, the two included trials used different control interventions STST (stretching and strengthening)
                                 and PRES (progressive running and eccentric strengthening) both of which represent conventional rehabilitation
                                 approaches. We considered pooling these comparisons clinically appropriate as both reflect standard care against
                                 which PATS was evaluated.

 www.nature.com/scientificreports

                                 time to return to play; WMD weighted mean difference; CI confidence interval.

                                 risk difference; CI confidence interval.



                                 TTRTP
                                 Two randomized controlled trials52,53 evaluated the effect of a PATS compared with STST or PRES on TTRTP
                                 following HSIs. A random-effects meta-analysis was performed due to moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 35%,
                                 P = 0.21). The pooled analysis showed no significant difference in TTRTP between the PATS group and the
                                 control groups, with a WMD of −6.72 days (95% CI −16.81 to 3.36, p = 0.19; Fig. 5). Sherry et al.53 reported a
                                 mean difference of − 15.20 days (95% CI −32.12 to 1.72) favoring PATS over STST, whereas Silder et al.52 found
                                 a smaller, non-significant difference of −3.60 days (95% CI −10.52 to 3.32) when comparing PATS with PRES.
                                 These findings indicate that, compared with conventional strengthening and stretching or eccentric running
                                 programs, the addition of progressive agility and trunk stabilization does not significantly accelerate return to
                                 sport after HSIs.

                                 Re-injury rate
                                 These two studies52,53 reported re-injury rate following PATS compared with STST or PRES. A random-effects
                                 meta-analysis using risk difference was conducted due to substantial heterogeneity (Tau² = 0.06; Chi² = 3.54,
                                 df = 1, P = 0.06; I² = 72%). The pooled analysis showed no statistically significant difference in re-injury rate
                                 between PATS and control groups (RD −0.35, 95% CI −0.74 to 0.03, p = 0.07; Fig. 6). Across both studies, two
                                 re-injuries occurred in the PATS groups (n = 29) compared with ten in the control groups (n = 24). Individual
                                 trial results ranged from RD −0.56 (95% CI −0.88 to −0.24) in Sherry et al.53 to RD −0.17 (95% CI −0.43 to 0.09)
                                 in Silder et al.52. A sensitivity analysis using Peto odds ratio (I² = 0%) yielded a larger effect estimate (OR 0.08,
                                 95% CI 0.02 to 0.38), but the statistical significance of this estimate should be interpreted with caution. The Peto
                                 odds ratio can produce unstable estimates in the presence of very large treatment effects and sparse event data,
                                 as is the case here. The primary analysis using risk difference (RD −0.35, 95% CI −0.74 to 0.03, p = 0.07) was
                                 statistically inconclusive, and the inconsistent findings across the two analytical approaches indicate that the
                                 evidence for PATS on re-injury prevention remains uncertain. We therefore emphasize the absolute event counts
                                 (2/29 vs. 10/24) and the width of the RD confidence interval, which crosses the null, as more informative than
                                 the point estimate of the Peto OR.

                                 Pain and Functional Outcomes
                                 Sherry et al.53 conducted a battery of functional tests at the TTRTP, including hop tests (hop for height, hop
                                 for distance, 4-hop crossover test) and 40-yard sprint times. No significant differences were observed between
                                 the PATS and STST groups for any functional measure (all p > 0.05). Furthermore, functional test performance
                                 did not differ between athletes who subsequently sustained a re-injury and those who did not (P = 0.07–0.97),
                                 suggesting that these tests had limited predictive value for re-injury risk. Silder et al.52 reported that at the
                                 TTRTP, nearly all subjects in both groups had resolution of pain with palpation and during manual muscle
                                 strength testing. However, 11 of 25 subjects (44%) who completed rehabilitation reported remaining hamstring
                                 symptoms (e.g. pain, tightness), with no significant difference between groups (7/13 in PATS vs. 4/12 in PRES,
                                 P = 0.444). Twelve subjects (48%) did not feel they had returned to their pre-injury level of performance, though
                                 only three (12%) attributed this limitation to their hamstring injury, with general deconditioning being the
                                 most common limiting factor. ROM measures (passive straight leg raise) showed no significant between-group
                                 differences at final examination (P = 0.337). Importantly, despite meeting clinical return-to-sport criteria (no
                                 pain, full strength), no subject in either group showed complete resolution of injury on MRI, indicating ongoing
                                 tissue healing52,53.
