 www.nature.com/scientificreports




                                 Fig. 7. Forest plot of the impact of PRP combined with rehabilitation versus rehabilitation alone (no injection)
                                 on TTRTP of HSIs; TTRTP time to return to play; WMD weighted mean difference; CI confidence interval.




                                 Fig. 8. Forest plot of the impact of PRP combined with rehabilitation versus rehabilitation alone (no injection)
                                 on re-injury rate of HSIs; RD risk difference; CI confidence interval.



                                    Taken together, these findings indicate that PATS and control programs yield comparable improvements in
                                 pain and functional performance at the TTRTP. However, residual symptoms and functional deficits may persist
                                 despite clinical clearance, underscoring the need for continued monitoring and gradual return to full activity.

                                 Rehabilitation programs combined with physical modalities
                                 Five randomized controlled trials39,56,57,59,61 evaluated the effect of rehabilitation programs combined with
                                 physical modalities on TTRTP following HSIs. Due to substantial differences in biological rationale, mechanism
                                 of action, and clinical objectives, we did not pool these interventions into a single estimate. Instead, we conducted
                                 a meta-analysis for PRP, for which three trials were available, and narratively described the single-trial evidence
                                 for rESWT and LLLT.

                                 Rehabilitation programs combined with PRP
                                 TTRTP
                                 A random-effects meta-analysis of the three PRP trials (PRP combined with rehabilitation versus rehabilitation
                                 alone or placebo injection) showed that PRP suggestively reduced TTRTP compared with control, with a
                                 weighted mean difference (WMD) of −6.77 days (95% CI −10.79 to −2.75, p = 0.0010; Fig. 7). Heterogeneity was
                                 substantial (I² = 70%, p = 0.03). Individual trial effects ranged from WMD − 4.00 days (95% CI −6.48 to −1.52)
                                 in Hamilton et al.39 to WMD − 15.80 days (95% CI −28.11 to −3.49) in Hamid et al.61, with Desouza et al.57
                                 reporting an intermediate effect (WMD − 7.80 days, 95% CI −10.40 to −5.20). The substantial heterogeneity may
                                 reflect differences in PRP preparation (leukocyte-rich versus leukocyte-poor), injection timing, rehabilitation
                                 protocols, or definitions of return to sport across studies.

                                 Re-injury rate
                                 The three PRP trials reported re-injury rates over follow-up periods ranging from 6 to 24 months. A fixed-effects
                                 meta-analysis (I² = 0%, p = 0.32) showed no significant difference between PRP and control groups (RD −0.08,
                                 95% CI −0.19 to 0.02, p = 0.13; Fig. 8). Across the three trials, three re-injuries occurred in the PRP groups
                                 (n = 56) versus eight in controls (n = 59). Sensitivity analyses using Peto OR (OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.12 to 1.34,
                                 p = 0.14) and random-effects models (OR 0.39, 95% CI 0.11 to 1.36) confirmed the null finding. Desouza et al.57
                                 reported one re-injury in the PRP group versus five in controls (RD −0.13, 95% CI −0.28 to 0.01); Hamilton et
                                 al.39 reported two versus three (RD −0.03, 95% CI −0.18 to 0.12); Hamid et al.61 reported no re-injuries in either
                                 group and did not contribute to the pooled estimate.

                                 Pain and functional outcomes
                                 Hamid et al.61 assessed pain using the Brief Pain Inventory-Short Form (BPI-SF). Patients in the PRP group
                                 demonstrated significantly lower pain severity scores across all follow up time points compared with controls (β
                                 = −0.390, 95% CI −0.67 to −0.11, p = 0.007). However, no significant between-group difference was observed for
                                 pain interference with daily activities (β = −0.185, 95% CI −0.44 to 0.07, p = 0.157). Hamilton et al.39 evaluated
                                 isokinetic knee flexor strength at return to sport and found no significant differences between PRP and control
                                 groups for concentric strength at 60°/s, 300°/s, or eccentric strength at 60°/s (all p > 0.05). Desouza et al.57 did not
                                 report standardized pain or functional outcome measures. Due to the heterogeneity in outcome reporting across
                                 studies, a quantitative synthesis for pain and functional outcomes was not feasible.


Scientific Reports |   (2026) 16:30859                | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-70693-1                                                   10
 www.nature.com/scientificreports


                                 Rehabilitation programs combined with rESWT
                                 TTRTP
                                 The rESWT group showed a significantly shorter TTRTP compared with the sham group (25.4 ± 3.5 days versus
                                 28.3 ± 4.5 days; mean difference − 2.90 days, 95% CI −5.63 to −0.17; SMD − 0.70, 95% CI −1.38 to −0.03).

                                 Re-injury rate
                                 One re-injury occurred in each group over the 6-month follow-up period (1/16 versus 1/16), with no significant
                                 between-group difference. Due to single-trial nature, formal meta-analysis was not performed.

                                 Pain and functional outcomes
                                 Crupnik et al.59 assessed isometric knee flexor strength post-treatment using two-way repeated measures
                                 ANOVA. A significant leg effect (previously injured versus contralateral uninjured leg) was observed (p = 0.005),
                                 but no significant treatment effect was detected (p = 0.899). Post-hoc testing showed that in the sham rESWT
                                 group, the previously injured leg was significantly weaker than the contralateral uninjured leg (p = 0.014),
                                 whereas no such difference was observed in the rESWT group. However, the treatment-by-leg interaction was
                                 not reported; therefore, these findings should be interpreted cautiously and do not establish that rESWT restores
                                 strength symmetry.

                                 Rehabilitation programs combined with LLLT
                                 TTRTP
                                 The study found no significant benefit of LLLT over placebo for TTRTP (mean difference − 0.80 days, 95% CI
                                 −11.22 to 9.62; SMD − 0.06, 95% CI −0.90 to 0.77).

                                 Re-injury rate
                                 No re-injuries occurred in either group during the 6-month follow-up period (0/11 versus 0/11). With zero
                                 events in both arms, the effect estimate was not estimable.

                                 Pain and functional outcomes
                                 Medeiros et al.56 assessed hamstring flexibility (passive straight leg raise, knee extension test, maximal hip flexion
                                 active knee extension) and isometric strength (inner, mid, and outer range) using a handheld dynamometer.
                                 Both the LLLT and placebo groups showed significant improvements over time (time effect p < 0.05), but no
                                 significant group-by-time interactions were observed for any flexibility or strength outcome (all p > 0.05), with
                                 between-group effect sizes ranging from trivial to moderate (Cohen’s d = 0.04–0.61). These findings indicate that
                                 LLLT provided no additional benefit over placebo for pain, flexibility, or strength recovery.

788	                                 decreased similarly in both groups, with no significant between-group differences. No adverse events occurred,
789	                                 and no rehabilitation-period reinjuries were reported. Thus, pain-threshold rehabilitation enhances strength at
790	                                 long muscle lengths and architectural adaptations without increasing fear or risk.

792	                                 Physical modalities
793	                                 TTRTP
794	                                 No data on TTRTP were available for stand-alone physical modalities. The included study focused on short-term
795	                                 (up to 48 h) symptomatic and functional outcomes without defining return-to-sport criteria or recording the
796	                                 time from injury to full sport participation25.
797	
798	                                 Re-injury rate
799	                                 The study did not systematically report hamstring re-injury rate. Kelli et al.25 did not follow participants beyond
800	                                 48 h after the single intervention session, precluding any assessment of injury recurrence.
801	
802	                                 Pain and functional outcomes
803	                                 Kelli et al.25 compared a single session of TECAR (n = 24), TENS (n = 26), or rest (n = 25) in athletes with acute
804	                                 HSIs. TECAR produced significantly greater reductions in VAS (−38.8% to −63.3%) and greater improvements
805	                                 in FASH (28.6–48.2%) and flexibility (SLR/STR) than TENS (−16.7% to −25.0% for VAS) or rest (all p < 0.05).
806	                                 These findings suggest that TECAR may offer short-term pain relief and functional improvement in the acute
807	                                 phase, although the long-term benefits remain unclear due to the absence of extended follow-up.
808	
809	                                 Stretching exercise
810	                                 TTRTP
811	                                 Only Malliaropoulos et al.60 reported a return-to-play relevant outcome: the time required for full rehabilitation
812	                                 (return to unrestricted athletic activities). The higher-frequency stretching group (Group B) achieved full
813	                                 rehabilitation significantly faster than the lower-frequency group (Group A) (mean ± SD: 13.27 ± 0.71 days vs.
814	                                 15.05 ± 0.81 days, p < 0.001). Additionally, the time to normalize active knee extension range of motion was
815	                                 shorter in Group B (5.57 ± 0.71 days vs. 7.32 ± 0.53 days, p < 0.001). Sefiddashti et al.55 did not report TTRTP. No
816	                                 meta-analysis was performed due to the absence of uniform TTRTP definitions across studies.

818	                                 Re-injury rate
819	                                 Neither study systematically reported hamstring re-injury rates. Malliaropoulos et al.60 followed athletes only
820	                                 until return to full training without providing long-term recurrence data. Sefiddashti et al.55 assessed outcomes
821	                                 immediately after the 5-day intervention period and did not report follow-up beyond the post-treatment
822	                                 assessment.

824	                                 Pain and functional outcomes
825	                                 Sefiddashti et al.55 assessed pain at rest and during activity using a 10-point VAS and functional status using
826	                                 the Lower Extremity Functional Scale (LEFS). Both the cryostretching (n = 18) and cryotherapy (n = 19) groups
827	                                 improved from baseline to post-treatment, but between-group differences were not significant for pain at
828	                                 rest or during activity (p > 0.05). For passive knee extension range of motion (PKE), the cryostretching group
829	                                 showed a significantly larger improvement than the cryotherapy group (p < 0.05), whereas improvements in
830	                                 active knee extension (AKE) did not differ significantly between groups. Functional status (LEFS) improved to a
831	                                 significantly greater extent in the cryostretching group compared with the cryotherapy group (p < 0.05), with the
832	                                 change exceeding the minimal detectable change (4.2 points), indicating a clinically meaningful improvement.

840	                                 used as a proxy for recovery of flexibility and functional capacity.
841	                                     Taken together, these findings suggest that incorporating static stretching into early rehabilitation,
842	                                 particularly when applied at higher frequency, accelerates the restoration of range of motion and shortens overall
843	                                 rehabilitation time. Cryostretching (ice plus stretching) provides additional benefits for passive flexibility and
844	                                 self-reported function compared with cryotherapy alone, without significant additional pain reduction.

846	                                 Spinal adjustive therapy
847	                                 TTRTP
848	                                 The study54 did not report time to return to play as an outcome measure. Therefore, no data were available for
849	                                 meta-analysis or qualitative synthesis for this outcome.

851	                                 Re-injury rate
852	                                 This study did not report re-injury rate. Follow-up was limited to the post-treatment assessment after the fifth
853	                                 session, with no long-term surveillance for injury recurrence.

855	                                 Pain and functional outcomes
856	                                 Using a Cybex system 2000, the primary outcome is hamstring muscle contractile strength during knee flexion.
857	                                 Although the groups had different baselines for contractile strength (due to age and body weight), both groups
858	                                 had increases in contractile strength after intervention. Group A (spinal adjustment + ultrasound) had greater
859	                                 increases in overall muscle contraction of the previously injured leg compared to Group B (ultrasound only).
860	                                 The study did not report pain scores (e.g. VAS) or functional status questionnaires. Due to no reported TTRTP,
861	                                 re-injury, or standardized pain/function measures, this study was excluded from the quantitative synthesis. The
862	                                 data indicate that spinal adjustment may provide more benefit to improving hamstring strength, yet further
863	                                 research with relevant clinical outcomes is needed.

865	                                 GRADE assessment
866	                                 The GRADE assessment revealed marked variability in evidence certainty across intervention categories and
867	                                 outcomes (Table 3). For TTRTP outcomes, downgrading for imprecision was applied when the 95% confidence
868	                                 interval crossed the MCID threshold of 7 days or when the optimal information size was not met; for re-injury
869	                                 outcomes, imprecision was assessed based on event counts and confidence interval width crossing the null.
870	                                 Inconsistency was downgraded when I² exceeded 50% and the direction of effects varied substantially, and
871	                                 risk of bias downgrades were based on the proportion of information from studies with “some concerns” or
872	                                 “high” RoB 2 ratings exceeding 33.3%. Moderate certainty evidence was confirmed for eccentric loading on
873	                                 TTRTP (downgraded solely for risk of bias), for Rehab + LLLT on TTRTP (downgraded for imprecision due
874	                                 to small sample size), and for pain-threshold rehabilitation on TTRTP (downgraded for risk of bias). Single-
875	                                 trial evidence does not automatically imply low certainty rather, certainty reflects the confidence in the effect
876	                                 estimate based on the trial’s methodological quality and precision. Low certainty evidence was observed for

878	                                 on both TTRTP (inconsistency, I² = 62%) and re-injury rate (imprecision), Rehab + rESWT on both TTRTP and
879	                                 re-injury rate (risk of bias and imprecision), Rehab + LLLT on re-injury rate (zero events, very small sample),
880	                                 and pain-threshold rehabilitation on re-injury rate (risk of bias and imprecision). PATS for re-injury reduction

882	                                 sequential analysis indicating inconclusive evidence. Collectively, these findings indicate that, aside from the
883	                                 TTRTP benefits of eccentric loading, Rehab + LLLT, and pain-threshold protocols (moderate certainty), most
884	                                 estimates remain provisional, underscoring an urgent need for high-quality, adequately powered RCTs to
885	                                 improve confidence in clinical recommendations.

887	                                 Discussion
888	                                 It is important to note that TTRTP alone should not be interpreted as a marker of complete recovery. Return
889	                                 to sport particularly return to competition or full performance requires restoration of strength, neuromuscular
890	                                 control, and sport-specific function, which may not be fully captured by TTRTP criteria alone. Throughout
891	                                 our GRADE assessment, we prioritized clinical relevance (whether the 95% CI crossed the 7-day MCID) over
892	                                 nominal statistical significance (whether p < 0.05), consistent with the principle that statistically significant

894	                                 imprecise but suggest potential benefit. Interpretation of the pooled TTRTP findings is further complicated by
895	                                 variation in return-to-play definitions across the included studies. These definitions ranged from return to full

                                     The cumulative Z-curve for the two PATS trials52,53 did not cross either the conventional threshold of 1.96

                                 information to meet the required information size. Although the point estimate favors PATS for re-injury
                                 reduction, the evidence is insufficient to eliminate the risk of random error; consequently, the observed risk
                                 reduction should be interpreted as preliminary rather than definitive, and further large-scale trials are warranted
                                 to confirm these findings.
                                     Trial sequential analysis was conducted for the three PRP trials comparing PRP combined with rehabilitation
                                 versus control39,57,61(Fig. 11). For TTRTP (Panel A), the cumulative Z-curve crossed the conventional boundary
                                 of 1.96 and reached the required information size, but did not cross the O’Brien-Fleming monitoring boundary.

                                 a narrative synthesis following the SWiM framework44. For each intervention, we report the direction of effect,

                                 TTRTP
                                 Median time from injury to TTRTP clearance was 15 days (95% CI 13 to 17) in the pain-free group and 17 days
                                 (95% CI 11 to 24) in the pain-threshold group. Hickey et al.58 reported the hazard ratio for achieving TTRTP
                                 clearance in the pain-threshold group relative to the pain-free group was 0.75 (95% CI 0.40 to 1.40, p = 0.37),
                                 indicating no significant difference between protocols. All participants in the pain-threshold group (21/21) and
                                 21 of 22 participants in the pain-free group met TTRTP clearance criteria.

                                 Re-injury rate
                                 Over the 6-month follow-up period after TTRTP clearance, two reinjuries occurred in each group (pain-free:
                                 2/22; pain-threshold: 2/21). The hazard ratio for re-injury in the pain-threshold group was 1.05 (95% CI 0.14 to
                                 7.47, p = 1.00), demonstrating no significant difference in recurrence risk between protocols.

                                 Pain and functional outcomes
                                 Hickey et al.58 compared isometric knee flexor strength, BFlh fascicle length, and fear of movement between
                                 pain-threshold (pain ≤ 4/10) and pain-free rehabilitation. At return-to-play clearance and 2-month follow-
                                 up, the pain-threshold group showed significantly greater strength recovery at 90° hip/90° knee flexion (mean
                                 difference 15% at both time points; 95% CI 1–28% and 1–29%, respectively). No between-group differences
                                 were observed at 0° hip/0° knee flexion. BFlh fascicle length increased more in the pain-threshold group from
                                 baseline to 2-month follow-up (mean difference 0.91 cm, 95% CI 0.34 to1.48). Fear of movement (Tampa Scale)
                                 decreased similarly in both groups, with no significant between-group differences. No adverse events occurred,
                                 and no rehabilitation-period reinjuries were reported. Thus, pain-threshold rehabilitation enhances strength at
                                 long muscle lengths and architectural adaptations without increasing fear or risk.

1001	                                 PATS are developed for a unique clinical focus: prevention of re-injury over the long-term. The results of our
1002	                                 meta-analysis indicate that PATS programs do not reduce TTRTP significantly compared to control programs

1004	                                 a clinically meaningful effect. The point estimate (RD −0.35) suggests a potential reduction, but the 95% CI
1005	                                 (−0.74 to 0.03) is wide and crosses the null; combined with very low certainty, high heterogeneity (I² = 72%), and
1006	                                 inconclusive TSA, this finding should not be interpreted as evidence of efficacy. The potential prophylactic effect
1007	                                 of PATS may be related to its capacity to address biomechanical and neuromuscular deficits, although mediator
1008	                                 data directly linking lumbopelvic control improvements to re-injury reduction are not available. Isolated
1009	                                 hamstring strengthening, while effective for restoring local muscle force-generating capacity, fails to remediate
1010	                                 the broader kinetic chain dysfunctions that contribute to tissue overload during sport-specific movements65–67. In
1011	                                 contrast, PATS incorporates progressive trunk stabilization exercises designed to enhance lumbopelvic control-a
1012	                                 factor increasingly recognized as integral to hamstring injury etiology. During the terminal swing phase of high-
1013	                                 speed running, the biceps femoris long head undergoes peak musculotendon strain while actively lengthening
1014	                                 to decelerate the lower limb. Insufficient lumbopelvic stability may allow excessive anterior pelvic tilt and trunk
1015	                                 rotation, increasing the eccentric demand on the hamstrings and predisposing the muscle to overload injury. By
1016	                                 improving lumbopelvic control, PATS may reduce compensatory pelvic motion and thereby mitigate eccentric
1017	                                 hamstring strain during high-velocity running movements. A narrative review by Badrinath et al.68 concluded
1018	                                 that athletes returning to sport after conventional rehabilitation exhibit persistent neuromuscular inhibition of
1019	                                 both the hamstring and lumbopelvic musculature, manifesting as impaired myoelectric activity in the biceps
1020	                                 femoris and altered activation patterns in the gluteal and trunk stabilizers. These residual deficits, undetectable
1021	                                 by standard clinical clearance criteria (pain-free palpation, full isometric strength), may explain the alarmingly
1022	                                 high early re-injury rates observed in protocols that neglect lumbopelvic retraining. The PATS re-injury analysis
1023	                                 illustrates the challenge of interpreting sparse event data. The primary RD analysis was inconclusive, whereas
1024	                                 the Peto OR sensitivity analysis suggested a large effect. This discrepancy likely reflects the instability of Peto
1025	                                 OR under extreme effect sizes and sparse events, as well as the marked difference in baseline risk between the
1026	                                 two studies. Given this uncertainty, the PATS finding should be considered hypothesis-generating rather than
1027	                                 confirmatory.
1028	                                     Despite the compelling evidence, important limitations temper clinical translation. Despite near-universal
1029	                                 acceptance of lumbo-pelvic training in elite sport, interventions exploring its effect on hamstring injury rates
1030	                                 have not measured stability in any meaningful way, and prospective risk factor studies examining lumbopelvic
1031	                                 motion during sprinting remain scarce69. Furthermore, the London International Consensus and Delphi Study
1032	                                 on hamstring injuries reported that 91% of experts agreed it is “important to assess, treat and prescribe exercises
1033	                                 addressing the whole kinetic chain”, yet consensus on specific exercise selection and progression criteria
1034	                                 remains elusive. Future trials must define standardized PATS protocols and evaluate whether individual patient
1035	                                 characteristics-including baseline lumbopelvic control, sport-specific biomechanical demands, and injury
1036	                                 chronicity-modulate treatment response.
1037	                                     Physical modalities-including PRP, rESWT, and LLLT are frequently employed as adjuncts to exercise-
1038	                                 based rehabilitation in athletes with hamstring strain injuries. However, these passive interventions do not
1039	                                 restore eccentric strength, neuromuscular control, or sport-specific functional movement patterns, which are
1040	                                 prerequisites for safe return to sport. Their appeal lies in the theoretical potential to modulate pain, accelerate
1041	                                 tissue repair, and create a permissive environment for early loading. However, despite decades of clinical
1042	                                 application, the evidence supporting their routine use remains inconsistent, and their role in hamstring strain
1043	                                 injury management continues to generate considerable debate. Our stratified analyses demonstrate that these
1044	                                 modalities should not be considered interchangeable. PRP has garnered particular interest due to its theoretical
1045	                                 capacity to deliver concentrated growth factors to the injury site. A systematic review of six RCTs (n = 277) from
1046	                                 2026 found that PRP reduced TTRTP by a mean difference of −8.6 days (95% CI −3.04 to −0.03, p = 0.045)
1047	                                 compared with control, though heterogeneity was high (I² = 94.1%) and re-injury rate did not differ (15% vs. 16%,
1048	                                 p = 0.722). Similarly, Liu et al.70 demonstrated shorter TTRTP with PRP plus physical therapy versus physical
1049	                                 therapy alone (MD −2.29, 95% CI −4.11 to −0.47, p = 0.01). Beyond PRP, Crupnik et al.59 reported that rESWT

1064	                                 continued rehabilitation through an exercise programme. Although PRP preparation protocols (leukocyte-rich
1065	                                 versus leukocyte-poor) and injection timing varied across the three trials, we considered pooling them clinically
1066	                                 appropriate because all evaluated PRP as an adjunct to structured rehabilitation in acute hamstring injuries, shared

1069	                                 PRP formulations and rehabilitation contexts, which limits the precision of the pooled estimate but does not
1070	                                 invalidate the overall direction of effect. The clinical heterogeneity across PRP studies, including differences in
1071	                                 injection protocols, rehabilitation programmes, and athlete populations, means that the pooled estimate should
1072	                                 be viewed as a summary of available evidence rather than a precise effect size applicable to all clinical settings.
1073	                                 Compared with recent systematic reviews10, which synthesized evidence on therapeutic exercises and modalities
1074	                                 without stratification, our review provides a stratified synthesis that separates exercise-based interventions
1075	                                 from adjunctive therapies. Unlike previous meta-analyses that pooled PRP across heterogeneous trials without
1076	                                 GRADE or TSA contextualization70, we analyzed PRP separately from other modalities and interpreted findings
1077	                                 according to evidence certainty rather than nominal statistical significance. Our findings on PRP are more
1078	                                 conservative than those reported in recent meta-analyses70, which generally reported statistically significant
1079	                                 effects based on pooled p-values without GRADE or TSA contextualization. This difference likely reflects our
1080	                                 stricter eligibility criteria (acute injuries only, excluding tendinopathy), our stratified analytical approach (PRP
1081	                                 analyzed separately from rESWT and LLLT), and our use of GRADE and TSA to distinguish suggestive from
1082	                                 definitive evidence. Our incremental contribution lies in this stratified, certainty-based interpretation rather
1083	                                 than in the identification of new primary studies.
1084	                                     Pain threshold rehabilitation appears to be an effective rehabilitation method that is safe. Hickey et al.58
1085	                                 did not find any cases of adverse events or re-injuries during rehabilitation and demonstrated a similar
1086	                                 decline in fear of movement scores in the two groups, suggesting that the presence of pain would not promote
1087	                                 kinesiophobia. The consistency of these findings with the larger body of literature on tendinopathy supports
1088	                                 the generalizability of the pain threshold principle for other forms of musculoskeletal injury72, although the
1089	                                 evidence for tendinopathy is indirect and should not be extrapolated to acute hamstring strains without caution.

1091	                                 acceptable; however, if pain continues or worsens, then the athlete’s loads should be reduced. The use of pain
1092	                                 threshold rehabilitation may reduce functional deficits and decrease the likelihood of future hamstring strains62.
1093	                                 Future studies are needed to determine if individual variables, such as injury severity, pain catastrophizing, and
1094	                                 psychosocial readiness, affect the optimal pain threshold, and whether recurrent injuries occur after 6 months
1095	                                 have passed. Overall, the available evidence supports that pain threshold rehabilitation is a safe, biologically
1096	                                 based method for improving tissue adaptation without slowing the recovery process or increasing injury risk.
1097	                                     The future of HSI rehabilitation lies in precision medicine: leveraging multimodal data streams to stratify
1098	                                 athletes by individual risk profiles and tailor interventions dynamically. Wearable sensors and AI may support
1099	                                 personalized rehabilitation, but standardized algorithms and sensor-placement protocols are currently lacking73.
1100	                                 Imaging biomarkers also show promise for objective injury assessment74,75, though translation into practice
1101	                                 requires standardized protocols and external validation76. These technologies are promising but remain in
1102	                                 development and were not evaluated in this review. Nevertheless, the convergence of risk stratification, wearable
1103	                                 monitoring, and AI-enabled analytics heralds a shift towards more personalized, technology-augmented care
1104	                                 pathways.

1109	                                 to blind participants and personnel in exercise-based trials. For re-injury outcomes, sparse events constrained

1114	                                 post-return sport exposure limited comparability; the small number of studies precluded formal subgroup

1116	                                 unreliable and requiring cautious interpretation of single-study and two-trial findings. The pooled L-protocol
1117	                                 TTRTP effect should be interpreted as population-specific rather than universally applicable, given the inclusion

1119	                                 largely absent, precluding meta-analysis. Female and recreational athletes were underrepresented. TSA revealed

1123	                                 therefore included only in narrative synthesis, consistent with our protocol. The English-language restriction

1126	 www.nature.com/scientificreports
1127	
1128	
1129	                                 may have contributed to language bias. Adherence to prescribed rehabilitation protocols was not uniformly

1140	                                 on clinical priorities, while acknowledging that current evidence does not identify a single strategy that reliably
1141	                                 optimizes both rapid return and durable protection. Future trials should use standardized injury and return-to-
1142	                                 sport definitions, report exposure-adjusted recurrence and adverse events, include sex-balanced samples, and
1143	                                 register protocols before recruitment.

                                 p = 0.722). Similarly, Liu et al.70 demonstrated shorter TTRTP with PRP plus physical therapy versus physical
                                 therapy alone (MD −2.29, 95% CI −4.11 to −0.47, p = 0.01). Beyond PRP, Crupnik et al.59 reported that rESWT

                                 added to an 8-week rehabilitation program reduced TTRTP by approximately three days (25.4 ± 3.5 vs. 28.3 ± 4.5
                                 days, p = 0.037) while preserving strength symmetry in the injured leg. While there are positive indicators to
                                 support their use, several caveats should be pointed out before recommending their use. This study was unable
                                 to conclude whether there are any clinical benefits from stretching programs or physical modality interventions
                                 according to Jankaew et al.71. The LLLT RCT also demonstrated no advantage over exercise, indicating that not
                                 all modalities provide equivalent benefits. Furthermore, heterogeneity among PRP preparation (leukocyte-rich,
                                 leukocyte-poor, activated, un-activated), injection times and image-guide protocols make interpretation more
                                 difficult. Standardized protocols and controlled trials comparing head-to-head the clinical effectiveness and cost
                                 effectiveness of the various modalities; if applicable, will further clarify those that are beneficial beyond optimal
                                 continued rehabilitation through an exercise programme. Although PRP preparation protocols (leukocyte-rich
                                 versus leukocyte-poor) and injection timing varied across the three trials, we considered pooling them clinically
                                 appropriate because all evaluated PRP as an adjunct to structured rehabilitation in acute hamstring injuries, shared
                                 comparable outcome definitions (time to return to sport), and used similar control conditions (rehabilitation
                                 alone or placebo injection). The substantial statistical heterogeneity (I² = 70%) reflects the clinical diversity in
                                 PRP formulations and rehabilitation contexts, which limits the precision of the pooled estimate but does not
                                 invalidate the overall direction of effect. The clinical heterogeneity across PRP studies, including differences in
                                 injection protocols, rehabilitation programmes, and athlete populations, means that the pooled estimate should
                                 be viewed as a summary of available evidence rather than a precise effect size applicable to all clinical settings.
                                 Compared with recent systematic reviews10, which synthesized evidence on therapeutic exercises and modalities
                                 without stratification, our review provides a stratified synthesis that separates exercise-based interventions
                                 from adjunctive therapies. Unlike previous meta-analyses that pooled PRP across heterogeneous trials without
                                 GRADE or TSA contextualization70, we analyzed PRP separately from other modalities and interpreted findings
                                 according to evidence certainty rather than nominal statistical significance. Our findings on PRP are more
                                 conservative than those reported in recent meta-analyses70, which generally reported statistically significant
                                 effects based on pooled p-values without GRADE or TSA contextualization. This difference likely reflects our
                                 stricter eligibility criteria (acute injuries only, excluding tendinopathy), our stratified analytical approach (PRP
                                 analyzed separately from rESWT and LLLT), and our use of GRADE and TSA to distinguish suggestive from
                                 definitive evidence. Our incremental contribution lies in this stratified, certainty-based interpretation rather
                                 than in the identification of new primary studies.

                                 did not find any cases of adverse events or re-injuries during rehabilitation and demonstrated a similar
                                 decline in fear of movement scores in the two groups, suggesting that the presence of pain would not promote
                                 kinesiophobia. The consistency of these findings with the larger body of literature on tendinopathy supports
                                 the generalizability of the pain threshold principle for other forms of musculoskeletal injury72, although the
                                 evidence for tendinopathy is indirect and should not be extrapolated to acute hamstring strains without caution.

                                 acceptable; however, if pain continues or worsens, then the athlete’s loads should be reduced. The use of pain
                                 threshold rehabilitation may reduce functional deficits and decrease the likelihood of future hamstring strains62.
                                 Future studies are needed to determine if individual variables, such as injury severity, pain catastrophizing, and
                                 psychosocial readiness, affect the optimal pain threshold, and whether recurrent injuries occur after 6 months
                                 have passed. Overall, the available evidence supports that pain threshold rehabilitation is a safe, biologically
                                 based method for improving tissue adaptation without slowing the recovery process or increasing injury risk.

                                 athletes by individual risk profiles and tailor interventions dynamically. Wearable sensors and AI may support
                                 personalized rehabilitation, but standardized algorithms and sensor-placement protocols are currently lacking73.
                                 Imaging biomarkers also show promise for objective injury assessment74,75, though translation into practice
                                 requires standardized protocols and external validation76. These technologies are promising but remain in
                                 development and were not evaluated in this review. Nevertheless, the convergence of risk stratification, wearable

 "paper": {
   "year": 2026,

   "doi": "10.1038/s41598-026-70693-1",
   "abstract": "Fourteen randomized controlled trials (693 athletes) were pooled to compare rehabilitation approaches for acute hamstring strain, with time to return to play (TTRTP) as the primary outcome and re-injury as the secondary outcome. A lengthening-focused protocol may shorten TTRTP with moderate certainty, while progressive agility and trunk stabilization, PRP, rESWT and LLLT remain uncertain for re-injury, and pain-threshold rehabilitation enhanced strength without delaying TTRTP.",
   "tldr": "A lengthening-focused eccentric protocol may shorten return to play after acute hamstring strain, supported by two trials with moderate certainty. Re-injury benefits from add-on approaches such as PATS, PRP and shockwave therapy are inconclusive or low certainty.",
   "methods": "Six databases (PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase and Google Scholar) were searched from inception to January 2026 for English-language RCTs of rehabilitation in athletes with acute hamstring strain. Risk of bias was rated with RoB 2 and certainty with GRADE, with random-effects models where clinical transitivity was judged adequate and trial sequential analysis as a robustness check.",
   "findings": "L-protocol (two trials, 131 athletes): TTRTP WMD -28.29 days (95% CI -41.60 to -14.99); re-injury RD -0.05 (95% CI -0.11 to 0.02), not significant.    "limitations": "Heterogeneity reached 72% for re-injury, blinding was not possible in exercise trials, and re-injury events were sparse, so TSA did not reach the required information size for PATS or PRP re-injury. The protocol was registered after the search was completed, and the authors' post-hoc split of physical modalities is noted.",
   "practicalImplications": "When getting an athlete back quickly is the priority after an acute hamstring strain, a lengthening-focused eccentric protocol is the best-supported option in this review, based on two mostly elite male trials.    "athleteDev": "The one trial with a strength outcome for pain-threshold rehabilitation found a 15% greater knee flexor strength gain at 90 degrees hip and knee flexion, with no slowing of return, under the authors' rule of pain 4/10 or less that settles within 24 hours.    "rtp": "The review informs timing only in part: the L-protocol was associated with earlier return to play, but the trials used varied return criteria and the authors warn that TTRTP is not a marker of full recovery. Clearance in the PATS trial still left residual symptoms in many athletes and no MRI-complete healing, so the review cannot set return-to-sport criteria; strength, neuromuscular control and sport-specific function should be checked as well."
 }
}

input.message:
Q01: INCLUDE | primaryDomain: Sports Medicine & Injury | Doubt: Systematic review/meta-analysis of sport-related concussion prevention (2025, Sports Medicine - Open 11:136). DOI printed in text. Populations tagged Male and Female Athletes because one included study (Peek et al.) is mixed-sex, though 7 of 8 studies are male-only; the Table 5 CI for physical training (0.42 to 0.89) differs from the text (0.41 to 0.89), and I used the table value and noted it.

Q02: INCLUDE | primaryDomain: Rehabilitation & Return to Sport | Doubt: Systematic review/meta-analysis of 14 RCTs on hamstring strain rehab (Scientific Reports 2026;16:30859). Own DOI 10.1038/s41598-026-70693-1 printed in the page header. Two judgement calls to check: (1) populations include "Adult / Recreational" for the amateur and semi-professional samples, which is a stretch; (2) the Discussion calls the PATS RD of -0.35 "clinically meaningful" while saying it is not evidence of efficacy, so I followed the Results/GRADE wording and flagged the conflict in limitations. Citation lists six authors then "et al." (seven authors in the text).
